title: 4.5-billion-year-old meteorite that crashed through Spring home's roof to go on display at Houston museum
excerpt: Remember the meteorite that crashed through the roof of a Spring home earlier this year? The 4.5-billion-year-old space rock is getting its own exhibit at the Houston Museum of Natural Science.
content:
Remember the meteorite that crashed through the roof of a Spring home earlier this year? The 4.5-billion-year-old space rock is getting its own exhibit at the Houston Museum of Natural Science.

The museum announced that its newest exhibition, "Fall To Earth," will feature the actual meteorite that crashed into Sherrie James' home on March 21, 2026. The exhibit opens Friday, Nov. 6, and will be free to the public.

James was inside her home when she heard a thunderous boom. She later discovered that a meteorite had torn through her roof, pierced an upstairs bedroom and landed near her daughter's bed.

The Ponderosa Fire Department initially investigated whether the object was debris from an aircraft, but its unusual weight and appearance suggested it was something else.

What started as a mysterious explosion heard across Southeast Texas turned into a rare opportunity for scientists to study material dating back to the formation of the solar system.

"This is one of those stories that almost seems impossible until you see it for yourself," said Dr. Carolyn Sumners, vice president of astronomy at the Houston Museum of Natural Science. "A 4.5-billion-year-old fragment of our solar system's original formation crashed through the roof of a Houston-area home. That's not something you expect to happen in your own neighborhood."

What scientists discovered about the meteorite

According to the museum, scientists estimate the original meteoroid entered Earth's atmosphere at nearly 35,000 mph, creating a fireball visible across much of Texas.

More than 180 eyewitnesses reported seeing the fireball, including people as far away as Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin and Rockport.

As the meteoroid broke apart above the Houston area, it released energy equivalent to approximately 26 tons of TNT. The resulting pressure wave rattled homes across Southeast Texas.

Weather radar also detected fragments falling toward Earth, helping scientists reconstruct the object's path.

Since the March incident, 19 meteorite fragments have been recovered throughout the Houston area.

Researchers at Rice University have proposed naming the meteorite "Houston" as part of the formal classification process. The name is awaiting approval from the Meteoritical Society.

NASA scientists also helped reconstruct the meteorite's journey through Earth's atmosphere.

Scientists have classified the meteorite as an ordinary chondrite, a type of stony meteorite that contains material dating back to the early solar system.

The meteorite is estimated to be 4.5 billion years old, making it nearly as old as Earth itself.

From a Spring home to a museum exhibit

The museum's new exhibition will give visitors an opportunity to see the meteorite up close while learning about its journey through space and the science behind its arrival in Spring.

Sumners said the exhibit will also highlight the unusual circumstances surrounding its discovery.

"This exhibition allows visitors to experience both the science behind the event and the remarkable human story that unfolded," she said.

For James, the experience remains one she never expected.

"It's just exciting to think of where it's been and how far it's traveled," James said. "That little thing has traveled by planets and stars, there's no telling how far it's come. So, it's very exciting. I just feel blessed it came to see me."
